seo.og_title: Solar panels and an electric car at home: how much they cover and what the prosumer law says
seo.og_description: The math for 10,000 km a year, net metering by tariff, the 10.8 kW cap and the December 31, 2026 deadline for new prosumers.

hero.h1: Solar panels and an electric car at home: how much they cover and what the prosumer law says
hero.lead: A rooftop plant of about 1.4–1.8 kW produces in a year roughly as much electricity as a car uses over 10,000 km. But panels work by day and mostly in summer, while a car usually charges at night, so under net metering the daytime surplus does not cover overnight charging.

card.title: Solar panels and an electric car at home
card.text: How much the roof covers, why daytime surplus does not cancel night charging and what applies after 2026.

blocks.p: Solar panels and a charger can work together, but the math is not a simple sum of kilowatt-hours. What decides it is when you charge, how the supplier settles the surplus and when you became a prosumer.

p: You can plan the panels and the charger separately. If you do not know yet where you will charge, start with the page

blocks.h2: How much the car uses and how much the roof gives

blocks.p: ADAC measured that the electric cars it tested in 2023 used 19.7 kWh per 100 km on average, and 21.1 kWh the year before. The example uses 20 kWh per 100 km and 10,000 km a year, which comes to about 2,000 kWh.
A 1 kW solar plant in Serbia produces roughly 1,100 to 1,400 kWh a year, depending on location, panel tilt and shade. For 2,000 kWh you need a plant of about 1.4 to 1.8 kW.

The same energy charged at night in the blue zone costs about 12,000 RSD a year, at a night rate of about 6 RSD per kWh. That is what those kWh would cost from the grid. Panels bring that saving only if a kWh from the roof really replaces a kWh from the grid.

blocks.h2: Sunshine and charging rarely line up

blocks.p: Panels produce the most in spring and summer and the least in fall and winter. Charging goes on all year, so in winter the roof covers a much smaller share of what the car uses.

The same goes for the time of day. Panels work while the sun is up, and the car is often at work or on the road then. When you plug it in in the evening, the roof no longer produces and all the charging power comes from the grid.

You can count on charging straight from the roof only when the car is at home by day: on weekends, on vacation or when you work from home. Then the charger's power matters too. A 1.4–1.8 kW plant never gives more than its rated power, even at noon, so an 11 kW charger takes most of its power from the grid. Charging at 2.3–3.7 kW is closer to what a small roof delivers.

The Law on the Use of Renewable Energy Sources defines a prosumer (kupac-proizvođač) as an end customer who has connected a renewable power plant to their own internal wiring. They use the power they produce first and feed the surplus into the grid.

Article 58 of that law, as amended in 2023, caps the plant's power. For a household the cap is 10.8 kW. If the connection is not three-phase, the cap is the power that matches a 10 A current, about 2.3 kW. The plant's power also cannot exceed the approved power of the connection.

In an apartment building, a single apartment cannot get this status. Only the residents' association (stambena zajednica) can, and only after a decision of its assembly. According to EDS data, in mid-2025 only five residents' associations in Serbia were registered with that status.

blocks.h2: Net metering: surplus carries over separately by tariff

blocks.p: A household prosumer today has a contract with net metering. When you feed in more than you draw in a month, the surplus carries over to the next month and reduces your consumption. The surplus is kept separately for the higher and for the lower tariff.

That is why daytime surplus does not cancel overnight charging. In EPS's sample bill, 1,602 kWh of surplus remains in the higher tariff after settlement, yet 270 kWh used in the lower tariff is still billed. Surplus you do not use by March 31 of the following year is canceled.

On your bill, watch the line „Viškovi za naredni obračunski period“ (surplus carried to the next period). If the higher-tariff surplus keeps growing, move part of your charging to daytime hours when you are at home. That way you use energy that would be lost on March 31. If you have no surplus, overnight charging at the lower tariff stays the cheapest.

blocks.h2: The December 31, 2026 deadline and net billing after it

blocks.p: The Energy Law provides that net metering for new prosumers is replaced by net billing by December 31, 2026 at the latest. The Ministry of Mining and Energy read the deadline this way: households that file a request to adapt the metering point by December 31, 2026 get net metering. Existing prosumers keep the settlement they already have.

Under net billing, the surplus no longer carries over in kilowatt-hours. Its value is settled in money under the contract with the supplier, and the energy you feed in is worth less than the power you draw. The rules for net billing have not been adopted yet, so the price of the surplus is not known either.

Article 131 of the Energy Law has several deadlines that are not clearly separated, and the ministry gave its reading in a reply, not in a regulation. So the safest order is this: file the request as early as you can, not in the last days of December, and keep proof of the filing date. If the plant cannot be finished in time, do the math as if you will have net billing.

blocks.h2: Steps for a house and what to check

blocks.p: For a household the procedure looks like this:

ul: You send the request to adapt the metering point to EDS online, with proof that the fee is paid.
You build the plant so that its power is not higher than the approved power of the connection.
You submit to EDS a certificate that the equipment and wiring are in order.
You sign a full-supply contract with net metering with EPS.
After the contract, the operator has five days to connect the site and another five days to enter you in the Register of prosumers.

blocks.p: Before you decide on panels, also check this:

ul: The approved power and the number of phases on your electricity bill. They set the largest plant and the charger power you can have.
Whether the plant and the charger can share one connection. A licensed electrician calculates that and does all work in the distribution board.
How many kWh the car really uses. A separate MID meter for the charger measures it, so you size the plant on real consumption, not on a guess.

p: The charger can go in before the panels and works the same with them or without them. Evolako START is a heavy-duty socket with a MID meter, 2.3–3.7 kW, and you can see all packages on the page
